result:
There is a place that doesn't exist on any map, and yet everyone has been there.

It's the place between places.

It's the airport at 6:47 AM when your flight doesn't board for another hour and you're suspended between where you were and where you're going. It's the last week of August before school starts again. It's the quiet moment after a song ends but before the applause begins. It's twilight, it's the shoreline where ocean stops pretending to be ocean and starts pretending to be land. We spend our lives trying to get from A to B as fast as possible, but we actually live most of our lives in the hyphen.

No one frames the hyphen and puts it on the wall. But maybe we should.

I have always been fascinated by waiting rooms. Not because I enjoy waiting - I don't, I'm terrible at it - but because of what happens to people while they wait. In a waiting room, the usual rules of society are gently suspended. Strangers who would never talk to each other on the street will strike up a conversation about the weather or the broken coffee machine or how long the doctor is taking. People read magazines they would never otherwise read. They stare out windows with a kind of unguarded openness. Their destination has them on pause, and in that pause, their public performance drops a little.

Anthropologists have a word for this: *liminal*. From the Latin *limen*, meaning threshold. The anthropologist Arnold van Gennep first described liminality over a hundred years ago when he was studying rites of passage. He noticed that in almost every culture, when someone is transitioning from one identity to another - from child to adult, from single to married, from civilian to soldier - there is a middle phase where they are neither. They are stripped of their old identity but not yet given the new one. They are in between. And in that in-between, something sacred and strange happens.

In many traditional societies, that liminal period was treated with incredible care. The initiates would be taken away from the village. They would wear special clothes, or no clothes. They would be given a new name, or no name at all. They were, for a brief time, nobody and everybody at once. Victor Turner, who expanded on van Gennep's work, called this state "communitas" - a spontaneous community of equals who are all equally in-between. Hierarchy disappears. If you've ever been on a delayed overnight flight where strangers share snacks and stories and phone chargers, you've felt communitas.

Modern life pretends we have eliminated liminality. We have tried to. We have built a world of instant gratification and seamless transitions. We stream the next episode without credits. We order food that arrives before we have time to get hungry. We scroll so we never have to be bored. We have made the hyphen as short and efficient as possible. And in doing so, we've lost something profound.

Because it turns out that humans need thresholds. We need hallways, not just rooms.

Think about twilight. Technically, it has no existence of its own. It's just the earth turning away from the sun, a scattering of light through atmosphere. But poets have obsessed over twilight for thousands of years precisely because it is neither day nor night. In twilight, the world is softer. Edges blur. The harsh contrasts of noon are gone. Colors become subtle. We see differently because the light is in-between. The Japanese have a term, *tasogare*, which literally means "who is that?" - because at dusk you cannot quite make out the faces of people approaching. Who is that? It's a question that belongs only to the threshold.

Or think about the shore. The intertidal zone is one of the most biologically productive and diverse places on the planet, not despite being in-between, but because of it. Twice a day it is drowned and twice a day it is exposed. Nothing that lives there can be purely a sea creature or purely a land creature. Mussels, barnacles, tidepool sculpins, sea stars - they are all specialists in ambiguity. They have to be tough and flexible and patient. Eccentric, too. Where else do you get a creature like a mudskipper, a fish that goes for a walk?

We are, all of us, intertidal creatures now. We live between analog and digital, between the world our parents prepared us for and the world that actually arrived. We live between childhood and old age for a surprisingly long time, that long middle stretch we call adulthood where we are old enough to know what we should do and young enough to still not do it. We live between who we present ourselves as online and who we are when the phone dies.

And the most quintessentially modern liminal space is, of course, the loading screen. That little wheel spinning, that bar inching forward. For a few seconds you are in a digital waiting room. You can't go forward and you can't go back. And what do we do? We hate it. We feel a flash of irritation utterly disproportionate to a three-second delay. We've been conditioned to believe that any threshold is a bug, not a feature.

But what if we treated it differently?

A few years ago I took a train across the country with no real purpose except to take a train across the country. It was three days. No Wi-Fi for most of it. No real schedule once I had boarded. I brought books, but after the first day I stopped reading them and just watched. America slid by at 60 miles an hour - backyards, rail yards, deserts, grain silos, small towns that seemed to exist just to be briefly seen from a train window. I talked to a man who was moving to Oregon to be closer to his daughter. I shared an apple with a kid who wasjl  bored. I slept badly and woke up to see the Rockies pink in the dawn. Nothing happened. And everything happened.

It was three days of pure hyphen. I wasn't at home and I wasn't at my destination. I had no role to play, no emails I could answer, no productive thing I could pretend to do. I was just in transit. And because I had no choice but to be there, I finally noticed how much of my ordinary life I spend trying to skip the transit part.

We treat life as if the important parts are the milestones - the graduations, the weddings, the promotions, the arrivals. We photograph those. We celebrate those. But the texture of a life is not in the milestones. It's in the thousands of unphotographed in-betweens. It's in the car rides where you have the real conversation. It's in the kitchen at 11 p.m. after the party is over and you're cleaning up with one other person. It's in the months after you quit a job but before you know what the next job is, when you are free and terrified and strangely alive.

The Buddhists have a concept called *bardo*, which is often translated as "intermediate state." Most famously it refers to the state between death and rebirth, but teachers will tell you that bardo is not just after you die. Every moment is a bardo. Every breath is a bardo between the last breath and the next. Waking up in the morning is a bardo. Falling asleep is a bardo. Any time you are between two thoughts, you are in a bardo. Enlightenment, they say, is not about escaping the bardo. It's about learning to rest in it.

That feels like the most useful advice I've ever heard. Learn to rest in the threshold.

How do you do that? Not easily, I think. Our instincts scream at us to rush. To define ourselves, to arrive, to know. Uncertainty feels physically uncomfortable, like an itch. We want to scratch it by making a decision, any decision. But the threshold has its own wisdom if you can stand to stay there a little while.

It teaches you that identity is not as solid as you thought. When you are between roles, you see that "you" are not the role. You are the thing that can inhabit different roles. It teaches you patience, which is not the same as waiting. Waiting is wanting to be somewhere else. Patience is being willing to be where you are. And it teaches you attention. When you are not focused on the destination, you finally look around at the hallway you're in. You notice the peeling paint, the strange window, the light coming in sideways.

So much beauty lives sideways.

If you are in an in-between right now - and you probably are, because everyone always is in some way - maybe don't hurry to get out of it. If you're between jobs, between relationships, between who you were and who you're becoming, between certainty and doubt. Don't pathologize it. Don't call it being stuck or lost or behind. Call it what it is: liminal. Call it intertidal. Call it twilight.

You are not lost. You are on the threshold. And thresholds are holy places.

They are where transformation actually happens, not at the start or the end, but in the messy, unmapped middle. The caterpillar doesn't become a butterfly by deciding to be a butterfly. It becomes a butterfly by dissolving into goo inside the chrysalis. For a while, it is neither caterpillar nor butterfly. It is soup. And then, impossibly, it reorganizes.

We all have our soup seasons. Honor them.

The world will keep telling you to optimize, to hustle, to arrive. Let it. You can smile and stay a little longer in the doorway anyway, feeling the draft from both sides, belonging to neither room and to both at once. The hyphen is where the sentence gets its meaning. Without it, you just have two words floating apart from each other, unrelated.

You are the hyphen. And that is not a small thing to be.
